candidates.statement: II. GENERAL PRINCIPLES 56 Information on a drug’s potential for abuse, misuse, addiction, physical dependence, and 57 tolerance is generally conveyed to health care providers in the DRUG ABUSE AND 58 DEPENDENCE section of labeling. Information about a product’s abuse-deterrent properties 59 should also be presented in this section. 60 The primary role of the DRUG ABUSE AND DEPENDENCE section of labeling is to convey 61 information about a drug’s potential for abuse, misuse, addiction, physical dependence, and 62 tolerance in order to help inform prescribing decisions and facilitate the safe and effective use of 63 prescription drug products. This section should be concisely and clearly written to include the 64 information that accurately summarizes the product’s abuse potential, signs and symptoms of 65 withdrawal, and abuse-deterrent properties (if applicable) and to provide information that is 66 important for the safe and effective use of the product. 67

candidates.statement: Generally, detailed information about drug abuse and dependence is included in the DRUG 71 ABUSE AND DEPENDENCE section of labeling. candidates.statement: A. 9.1 Controlled Substance 124 Under the CSA, controlled substances are placed in one of five schedules based on their potential 125 for abuse, whether they have a currently accepted medical use in the United States, and the 126 degree of dependence that abuse of the drug or other substance may cause. 8 Drugs in each 127 schedule are subject to a set of requirements governing their manufacture, distribution, and 128 dispensing, among other things. In general, the requirements that are most restrictive apply to 129 drugs scheduled in Schedule I and II; and those that are relatively less restrictive cover drugs 130 scheduled in Schedule III, IV, and V. 131
candidates.context: The DRUG ABUSE AND DEPENDENCE section is composed of three subsections 120 (§ 201.57(c)(10)). This information 136 should be conveyed in a single sentence. For example: 137 • DRUG-X contains active ingredient-Y, a Schedule II controlled substance. 138

candidates.statement: C. 9.3 Dependence 342 This subsection of labeling must contain, as appropriate, information about the drug related to 343 physical dependence, withdrawal, and tolerance. Under § 201.57(c)(10)(iii), the subsection must 344 describe characteristic effects resulting from the psychological and physical dependence that 345 occurs with the drug and must identify, if known, the quantity of the drug over a period of time 346 that may lead to tolerance or dependence, or both. 16 The Dependence subsection should 347 summarize signs and symptoms of withdrawal after chronic use or abuse of the drug, whereas the 348 Abuse subsection should discuss abuse-related adverse reactions. Procedures necessary to 349 diagnose the dependent state and the principles of treating or mitigating the effects of abrupt 350 withdrawal must be described in this subsection (§ 201.57(c)(10)(iii)). 351 This subsection should summarize the information that supports recommendations to health care 352 providers on how to prevent or mitigate risks associated with physical dependence, withdrawal, 353 and tolerance. Other sections of labeling that discuss clinical implications related to dependence 354 (e.g., DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION or WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS) should 355 cross-reference to the Dependence subsection as appropriate. 356

candidates.statement: 16 Terminology used to describe substance-related disorders continues to evolve, and a lexicon is being adopted in which past categories of substance abuse and substance dependence (as described in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fourth Edition (DSM-IV)) are combined into an overarching diagnosis of substance use disorder (as described in DSM-5), which is measured on a continuum from mild to severe. Accordingly, information about substance use disorders is generally parsed out between subsections 9.2 Abuse and 9.3 Dependence . Although addiction has historically been associated with the concept of psychological dependence, for the purposes of labeling, discussions related to addiction should appear in subsection 9.2 Abuse because addiction as it is currently understood relates more closely to abuse than to the subject matter discussed in 9.3 Dependence .
candidates.context: The appearance of a withdrawal syndrome when administration of the drug is terminated or 364 when an antagonist is administered is the only actual evidence of physical dependence. Physical 365 dependence is associated not only with the repeated use of known drugs of abuse, but with drugs 366 with no abuse potential as well. For example, physical dependence to propranolol (a beta- 367 blocker used for the management of hypertension) is known to occur, and abrupt discontinuation 368 may be followed by a “propranolol withdrawal syndrome” resulting in increased blood pressure 369 (temporarily higher than before starting propranolol), headache, chest pain, palpitations, and 370 sweating. 371 In a person who is physically dependent on a drug, a withdrawal syndrome is normally 372 anticipated when the drug is abruptly withdrawn, when the dose is reduced, or when the patient 373 is administered

candidates.statement: 2. Information on Tolerance 390 For drugs to which patients may develop tolerance, the following single sentence should be 391 included in the Dependence subsection: 392 • Tolerance is a physiological state characterized by a reduced response to a drug after 393 repeated administration (i.e., a higher dose of a drug is required to produce the same 394 effect that was once obtained at a lower dose). 395
candidates.context: • Discontinue DRUG-X by gradual taper over a 2-week period to reduce the risk of 387 symptoms of withdrawal [see Dosage and Administration (2.x)]. 388 Tolerance may develop to some drug effects much more rapidly than to other effects of the same 397 drug. For example, an individual might develop tolerance to the euphoria that opioids may 398 induce; however, the subject might not develop tolerance to the respiratory depressant effects of 399 the same opioid.
